title: Finding What Nobody Has Found: Zero-Days & Bug Hunting
mindset: Every program carries assumptions about its input; a researcher's job is to find the one the developer never imagined.

cards.title: Zero-day vs n-day, again
cards.body: A **zero-day** is a vulnerability the vendor does not know about yet, so defenders have had 'zero days' to fix it. Once a patch is out, it becomes an **n-day**: known and fixable, but only on systems that actually install the patch. Most real breaches use n-days, because patching is slow. Think of a lock flaw: a zero-day is one only the burglar knows; an n-day was in the newspaper, but half the street hasn't changed their locks yet.

cards.title: What vulnerability research is
cards.body: **Vulnerability research** is the craft of finding new security bugs in software. Researchers read source code, reverse-engineer programs (study compiled code to understand it), and test inputs the developer did not expect. It is like a building inspector who tries every window, crawls into the vents and reads the blueprints, asking 'what if?'. The core question is always: **where does untrusted input enter, and what does the program assume about it?** Parsers of files, images and network protocols are favourite targets.

cards.title: Fuzzing: automated 'what if?'
cards.body: **Fuzzing** feeds a program huge numbers of automatically mutated inputs and watches for crashes. A crash often means memory was handled wrongly, which can be a security bug. Modern fuzzers like **AFL++** and **libFuzzer** are **coverage-guided**: they notice which inputs reach new parts of the code and mutate those further. Imagine a robot pressing every button combination on a vending machine, remembering which ones made new noises, until one makes it spit out free snacks.

cards.title: Sanitizers: making bugs loud
cards.body: Many memory bugs do not crash immediately; they silently corrupt data. **Sanitizers** are compiler add-ons that make such bugs crash loudly with a clear report. **AddressSanitizer (ASan)**, turned on with `-fsanitize=address` in gcc or clang, catches reading or writing outside a buffer and using memory after it was freed. It is like adding dye to water pipes so a tiny leak becomes an obvious stain. Fuzzing plus sanitizers is the standard combination.

cards.title: Patch diffing: reading the fix to find the flaw
cards.body: When a vendor releases a security patch, attackers compare the old and new versions. This is **patch diffing**. Whatever changed around the fix points straight at the bug, so they can build an exploit for unpatched systems, sometimes within hours or days. It is like seeing a shop suddenly add bars to one particular window: now every thief knows which window was weak. This is why 'Patch Tuesday' is often followed by fast exploitation, and why patching speed matters.

cards.title: Responsible (coordinated) disclosure
cards.body: Found a bug? **Coordinated disclosure** means privately reporting it to the vendor, giving them time to fix it (commonly **90 days**, as popularised by Google Project Zero), then publishing details after the patch. Look for a `security.txt` file, a security email, or a bug bounty page. Do not access more data than needed to prove the issue, and never demand payment as a condition. That is extortion. A **CVE** ID can be requested through the vendor or a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority).

cards.title: Bug bounty methodology
cards.body:
A **bug bounty** is a programme where companies pay for valid vulnerability reports, run on platforms like HackerOne, Bugcrowd and Intigriti. The method:
1. **Read the scope and rules** first; out-of-scope testing is unauthorised.
2. **Recon**: map subdomains, endpoints and features.
3. **Understand the app** like a user.
4. **Test assumptions**: access control, inputs, logic.
5. **Write a clear report** with steps to reproduce and impact.
Duplicates are common, so depth on one target often beats shallow testing on many.

attacks.name: N-day exploitation after patch release
attacks.analogy: Reading the town notice that says 'the bank's back door lock is faulty and will be replaced next month', then visiting the banks that haven't replaced it yet.
how: Vendor publishes a patch and advisory.
Attacker diffs the patched and unpatched versions to locate the flaw.
Scans the internet for unpatched systems and exploits them at scale.
attacks.thinking: The vendor just told the world where the weakness is. How many organisations will take weeks to patch?
attacks.signs: Spike in scanning for the affected product right after an advisory, exploit attempts matching new IDS signatures, the CVE added to CISA's KEV catalogue.
attacks.defend: Asset inventory so you know what you run, prioritise internet-facing and KEV-listed vulnerabilities, patch within days, virtual patching (WAF/IPS rules) while waiting.

story.title: Heartbleed (2014)
story.body: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) was a bug in OpenSSL's 'heartbeat' feature, which lets one side say 'send back these 5 letters' to check the connection is alive. OpenSSL trusted the requested length without checking it, so an attacker could ask for up to 64 KB and receive leftover memory: passwords, session cookies, even private keys. It was found independently by Neel Mehta of Google and by Codenomicon, whose team found it while improving their testing tools. Around two-thirds of web servers used OpenSSL. Lesson: a single missing bounds check in widely shared code affects the whole internet, and systematic testing finds what code review misses.

lab.title: Fuzz your own buggy program with AFL++
lab.goal: Watch a coverage-guided fuzzer discover a hidden crash in a tiny program you write, then compare two versions of code like a patch differ.
steps: Install AFL++ and write a tiny C program that crashes on one secret input (the commands below do this).
Compile it with AFL++'s compiler so the fuzzer can see code coverage.
Give the fuzzer a harmless seed input and start fuzzing.
Within minutes, check the crashes folder and read the input that triggered it.
Write a fixed version and use `diff` to see what a patch differ would see.

commands.cmd: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y afl++ gcc
commands.explain: Installs AFL++ (the fuzzer, package name `afl++`) and the gcc compiler.

Writes `target.c`: it reads up to 7 bytes and deliberately crashes (`abort()`) only if the input starts with bytes 66, 85, 71, which are the letters `B`, `U`, `G`. This simulates a hidden bug; each nested `if` is a new branch the fuzzer can discover one letter at a time.

commands.cmd: afl-cc -o target target.c && mkdir -p in && echo hello > in/seed
commands.explain: `afl-cc` compiles the program with coverage tracking so the fuzzer knows which branches each input reaches. The `in` folder holds the starting (seed) input.

Starts fuzzing: `-i` seed folder, `-o` results folder, after `--` the program to test (input goes to its stdin). The two variables skip system-tuning checks for a quick lab. Press Ctrl+C once 'saved crashes' is above 0.
`xxd` shows the crashing input as bytes and text. You should see it begins with `BUG`: the fuzzer found it by itself by following new code paths.

commands.cmd: sed 's/abort();/puts("rejected");/' target.c > fixed.c && diff -u target.c fixed.c
commands.explain: Creates a 'patched' version and shows the difference. Patch diffing works the same way: the changed lines reveal exactly where the bug was.

lab.safety: Fuzz only programs you wrote or have the right to test, on your own machine. Never fuzz or probe live websites or services outside a bug bounty scope that explicitly allows it, and follow the programme's rules on automated testing.

hunt:
A researcher finds that changing `user_id=1001` to `1002` in a company's app shows another customer's invoice. To 'prove impact', they download 50,000 invoices, then email the company: 'Pay $10,000 or I publish them.' What is wrong?

Answer: The bug (an IDOR) was real and reportable, but the researcher went far beyond proof: one or two records are enough to demonstrate impact. Mass downloading is unauthorised data access, and demanding payment is extortion, a crime. Correct path: check for a bug bounty or `security.txt`, stop at minimal proof, report privately with clear steps, delete any data accessed, and allow time to fix.

terms.def: A vulnerability unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.
terms.use: "It was exploited as a zero-day before the vendor's emergency patch."

terms.def: Automatically sending many malformed or random inputs to a program to find crashes and bugs.
terms.use: "We fuzz the file parser in CI so new crashes are caught before release."

terms.def: Comparing software before and after a security fix to find exactly what was vulnerable.
terms.use: "Expect a public exploit soon; researchers are already patch diffing it."

terms.def: Privately reporting a vulnerability to the vendor and agreeing on when details are made public.
terms.use: "We followed coordinated disclosure with a 90-day deadline."

terms.def: A programme where organisations reward people for reporting valid vulnerabilities within a defined scope.
terms.use: "That subdomain is out of scope for the bug bounty, so don't touch it."

terms.def: A minimal demonstration that a vulnerability is real and exploitable.
terms.use: "Attach a PoC request in the report so triage can reproduce it quickly."

options: Only sends random bytes forever
Keeps and mutates inputs that reach new parts of the code
Reads source code for comments
Scans networks for open ports
quiz.why: Tracking code coverage lets the fuzzer explore deeper paths instead of guessing blindly.

quiz.q: Why do attackers patch-diff security updates?
options: To install them faster
To check the vendor's code style
The changed code reveals the vulnerability, so they can exploit unpatched systems
To find zero-days in other vendors
quiz.why: A patch is a map to the bug; unpatched systems become n-day targets.

quiz.q: What was the core flaw behind Heartbleed?
options: OpenSSL trusted a length value from the request without checking it
A weak password on a server
A phishing email to OpenSSL developers
An expired TLS certificate
quiz.why: Missing bounds checking let attackers read up to 64 KB of server memory per request.

quiz.q: You find a serious bug on a site with no bug bounty. What is the right first step?
options: Post it on social media
Exploit it fully to prove impact
Sell it to the highest bidder
Stop testing, look for security.txt or a security contact, and report privately
quiz.why: Coordinated disclosure protects users and you; going further without permission can be illegal.

options: Encrypting program memory
Making silent memory errors crash loudly with a report
Speeding up programs
Hiding bugs from attackers
quiz.why: ASan detects out-of-bounds and use-after-free errors that might otherwise go unnoticed.

talk.scenario: A colleague asks: 'If no one has published an exploit for this new CVE, can we wait until next quarter to patch?'
talk.model: I wouldn't wait. Once a patch is public, attackers can patch-diff it and build an exploit within days, which turns this into an n-day that's actively scanned for. If the system is internet-facing or the CVE lands on CISA's KEV list, it should be patched within days, not months. If we truly can't patch, we should add a compensating control like a WAF or IPS rule and watch for exploit attempts.

reflect: Think of an app or device you use daily. Where does it take input from strangers, and what assumption might its developers have made about that input?
